Hon. T. A. LOW (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 113, respecting Grain.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to enter a protest against the concurrence of this House particularly in one of the amendments made by the Senate to the bill as it was approved of in this chamber. I refer to the amendment made to section 140.
It is not necessary for me, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize the fact that throughout western Canada, where the great bulk of our wheat is produced, the opinion is prevalent that the process of mixing, which is a process adopted by those who market the grain, and not by the producers, is detrimental to the best interests of the producer in that his grain thus mixed reaches the final market in a condition not as pure, and with a grade not as high, as that which it has when it leaves the farm. When the bill was before this House I moved an amendment to section 140 which required that grain coming out of the mixing elevators

Elections Act
should be judged on a standard equal to that in Winnipeg, not on the lowest of the standards that is passed in Winnipeg, but on the average of that standard. That amendment was approved by this House, but the upper body, in its wisdom, has seein fit to reject that amendment that this House approved of, and to insert in its place a section which does not require that the grain coming out of the mixing elevator shall be of a grade equal to the average grade of the grain passing inspection at Winnipeg.
It is my opinion, Sir, that if the grain as it comes from the mixing elevator were required to be of a standard equal to the average of the standard on which the farmer's grain is inspected, at least the greater part of the objection to mixing would be done away with. I am informed by those who are well acquainted with this process of mixing that to require the mixing elevators to reach such a standard would practically do away with their business; the profit would be gone, and consequently mixing to a great extent would be stopped. If that would be the result, then, Sir, I would be willing to take the result of my amendment and I submit to this House that the producers of Canada would be behind us in that stand. If the profit is secured by bringing the grade lower than the average of the grade the farmer secures, the mixing elevators are taking an undue profit out of us and damaging our product before it reaches the final market.
It is said that my amendment is impracticable, that it could mot be worked. Well, Sir, if that is true I submit this, that it is a good way to prohibit something that should not be carried on. It is a fact that there are every year a number of bushels of low grade grain produced, and a very considerable quantity in some years. I am of the opinion that the privilege to mix this grain is a special privilege granted to companies operating elevators with a license to engage in this process, as a system by which this low grade grain is 'absorbed into the market with perhaps greater facility; but if iin absorbing the lower grades of grain we are to seriously deteriorate the higher grades of our grain and lower its value in the ultimate market-the Liverpool market-I submit we are doing something that is wholly contrary to the best interests of the producers. All that the amendment that was made in this House called for was that the product from the mixing elevator should be equal to the average of the grade which the farmer secures for his product from the farm. We are granting not only a special privilege in mixing, but if
we approve, as the government mow moves to approve, of the amendment made by the upper chamber, we are also granting a special privilege to the mixing elevator enabling them to ship out a product which is lower in grade than the average which the producer himself receives.
In making this protest, Mr. Speaker, I speak for at least the majority of those sitting around me, and I believe a very considerable majority, and we want our protest om record because we represent in this House first of all the producers of this country.
Motion agreed to on division; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

The House resumed from June 25th consideration in committee of Bill No. 148, to amend the Dominion Elections Act-Mr. Copp -Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 5-Use of provincial voters' list.

I would like to make sure as to the meaning of the words "provincial lists" in this section. Under the law as it stands, all elections for the Dominion House -I am referring now to the province of Ontario-would be held under lists used in provincial elections unless they were more than two years old. For example, should an election be held this fall we could not use the provincial lists used in the last provincial election and some other provision would have to be made. I understand that a list would be prepared from another list which would be used with or without revision at a provincial election commenced at the same time as the election under this act. That is, under conditions such as would prevail if we had an election this fall, with no old provincial lists available because they are more than two years old, we would then, I understand, have to take as a basis a list which would be used by the provincial government for the purpose of making a new list. If that is the case then I assume we would have to fall back upon what I would term the municipal lists, that is, lists prepared by the municipal officers as a basis for making a new list. In line 2 of subsection (a) it says: "Every urban registrar shall transfer from such provincial lists," and so on. Ordinarily I think the layman would call that a municipal list, and what I am concerned about is whether when we speak here of "provincial list" it does refer to the list that is prepared by the municipal officers, so that it may be definitely understood that in case of an election this fall or before a pro-

Elections Act
vincial election is held, our election list in Ontario will have as its basis the lists prepared by the municipal officers.

I put that question to the Chief Electoral Officer and he informs me that the term "provincial lists" refers to the lists made up according to the laws of the province for use in connection with the provincial elections. Provincial list does not necessarily mean a list made up by the province. It is made up by the municipalities and the list made up in that way would be the one used for provincial elections.
It is based on the municipal list?

Yes. I wish to move the following amendment:
That section 5 of the bill be amended by adding thereto as subsection 3 the following:
" If any question arises as to whether any list, or which of two or more lists, prepared under the laws of a province, should be used pursuant to such laws at a provincial election commenced at the same time as the election under this act, the Chief Electoral Officer may direct the use under this section of such list as should in his opinion be used, and such list shall be used accordingly."

If a list is found unsuitable will the Chief Electoral Officer have authority to change the whole basis, that is, make a change in the lists as used generally, or only in regard to the municipality in which the disability exists?
Just in relation to the municipality where the disability exists.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
Mr. COPP moved the third reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have on previous occasions, presented to the House as clearly and forcefully as I could the discrimination which subsection 1 of section 10 of the Dominion Elections Act imposes on organized labour. I have shown that owing to the nature of the trades union organization it is impractical for every trade union of every city to become incorporated for political purposes as is required by the act. In addition to the difficulty presented by the nature of the organization itself, I have shown that the constitu-* tion of the international trades union movement is an added barrier to the compliance of unions with clause 10 of the act. I introduced a bill early in the session to repeal the section in question. The government defeated that bill on the ground that to repeal the section would open the door to corruption, a view-

point which, if warranted by facts, is a damning indictment both of the wealthy people and of the common people of the country. The implications of this view are that certain wealthy people are both capable and desirous of corrupting the electorate, and also that the masses of the people are corruptible, and that both require the grandmotherly supervision of a statutory declaration. I use the term "statutory declaration" advisedly, for not only do I dissent from the view that our wealthy people who subscribe to election funds do so for the purpose of corruption, and that the average man is corruptible by such funds, but I hold the view that it would be, comparatively speaking, an easy matter for wealthy corporations to contribute through individuals for election funds notwithstanding the fact that such is prohibited by section 10 of the Act. Indeed I would not be surprised if in the next election a very great deal of the election funds for all parties should come from corporations- all parties, of course, with the exception of the Labour party. I have not much hope of the Labour party securing very heavy donations from the industrial controllers of this country or from the financial institutions. In any event, clause 10 of the Dominion Elections Act is only an impious statutory declaration. I believe it is violated by all concerned in every election, yet not a single prosecution has ever been instituted under its provisions. I submit to the House that to retain a section in an act which cannot be enforced-no; worse than that, which invites its own violation-is to bring law itself into disrepute. In fact, a law which people regard as one to be got around is more detrimental by far to parliamentary dignity than a shirtsleeves statesman to the presence of whom objection has been taken.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my colleague and I, believing that every individual or group of individuals, rich or poor, should be free to contribute funds for political purposes, providing that such funds be expended in legitimate channels or within the provisions of the act in this regard, accordingly made an attempt to repeal this legislation. But the government prevented us. Then we tried to amend the offending section by moving an amendment which would exempt labour unions. Having been defeated in our attempt to exempt all classes from the prohibition of the clause referred to, we took a course which would exempt labour alone, not however in any sense desiring class advantage but because labour unions are put to a greater disadvantage in violating the provision than any other class. But in this too we were defeated in com-

Elections Act
mittee of the whole. I now make a last effort to remove from the Dominion Elections Act, the discrimination against labour unions. But before moving an amendment to the bill before the House I desire to call the attention of organized labour throughout the country to the fact that the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and those around him have expressed their willingness to repeal clause 10 or, failing that, to support the amendment which I moved in committee. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) and his followers have expressed themselves also in a fashion similar to that of the opposition. For some strange reason rot yet given to parliament the government and their supporters doggedly refuse to add one phrase to a single clause of a single act which would remove an injustice to which labour is subjected.
Why is this? Is it because the government desires to hamper the political activities of labour men? One would be justified under the circumstances in that conclusion. But this petty oppression, in addition to being far from harmonizing with the theoretical principles of Liberalism, will not drive labour from the political field, although it will be a very considerable inconvenience. Perhaps the reason for the government's opposition to this amendment is that it was moved 'by the labour representatives in this House. I am loath to attribute to the government of Canada an attitude of mind as cantankerous and unfair as that. However, the fate of the amendment which I am about to move is in the hands of the government. I make an earnest-appeal to the common sense, the fairness and the generosity of the administration to support it. But if the government persists in its bovine obstinacy it must be lacking in these qualities to which I have appealed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my hoD. friend think that an expression like " bovine obstinacy " is calculated to induce the government to change its point of view?
I have merely described as best I can the attitude so far shown by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government is always prepared to meet hon. gentlemen opposite but will absolutely refuse to consider anything brought forward in a spirit such as characterizes this amendment.

If an expression of that description, however objectionable it may be to the administration, is sufficient to stand between the government and the performance 317
of its duty, then I shall have to describe the government's attitude further and more accurately. I was not using the expression in any objectionable sense but if the government objects to it I shall be glad to withdraw it. The amendment I am about to move-
Too late.

Yes, I presume it is too late. The second remark of the Prime Minister makes me despair of the administration paying the slightest attention to any appeal of labour; but I shall make that appeal nevertheless. There is no reason why a provision which is violated should not be removed, and the offending clause works more hardship on labour than on anybody else. If the government does not particularly want to stand in the way of labour, then I plead with hon. gentlemen opposite to remove the discrimination that now exists by adopting the amendment I move, seconded by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth):
That this bill be not read .the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions to amend subsection (1) of section 10 of the Dominion Elections Act by inserting the words " or a labour union " after the word " alone " in the third line thereof.

During the previous discussion of this matter I was unavoidably absent and I wish to take up the time of the House for a moment now to support the amendment. There is no doubt that organized labour throughout the country is placed under a serious and unfair handicap by the existing law. It is said that the present law was formulated many years ago by the Liberal party with a view to certain advantages which political organizations in Ontario would obtain. May I suggest that from our everyday contact with the public life of the country it is palpably unfair and unreasonable to handicap such a body of men and women as organized labour in Canada by a law which can bring little actual tangible good while in its operation it is capable of doing considerable actual tangible harm to these people. I was somewhat surprised at the way in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) received a certain remark made by the hon. member who has moved the amendment, and -I say this without the slightest intention of offending-I doubted the sincerity of the right hon. gentleman in his irritation over that remark. I do not think the Prime Minister will allow for one moment the words of any hon. member on any great measure affecting the masses of the people to interfere either with

Elections Act

the performance of his duty or with the carrying out of his good judgment in the interests of the country at large. I hope the government will reconsider the matter and that the present legislation, which has existed too long, be replaced by a far more sensible law in the interests of organized labour and of the people generally.

I have
taken this matter up with some labour men in Kamloops, and I may say that a certain percentage of them are opposed to it. They say that all labour men do not believe in sending labour members down here, some of the labour people belong to the Conservative and some to the Liberal party, and these men ask, why should they supply money to any candidate if they do not want to support him? Why should they be obliged to support financially anyone who is not of their persuasion? If the hon. member (Mr. Irvine) would move that the vote in the labour unions would have to be carried by a two-thirds majority I would support the motion; but I certainly cannot support it as it stands, in view of the instructions I have got from those I represent.
Will the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) give the name of one labour organization that he knows of in Canada that believes in what he says right now?

I did not state that I had discussed the question with the labour organizations, but I said that there was a number of gentlemen whom I knew belonged to the organization with whom I talked the matter over, and these men supported me and sent me down here, and it is their wishes I want to support.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary): I have had an opportunity of observing the hardship which is imposed upon labour unions by virtue of the provisions of the act which is now in force. The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) on a former occasion sought to strike out the section, in order that it might operate to the equal advantage or disadvantage, as the case might be, of all classes of the community. In its judgment the House saw fit to reject that proposition. The hon. member for East Calgary now asks in his amendment that labour unions be exempted from the operation of this section. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the section as it now stands does operate to the especial disadvantage of labour. I think the House will be well advised to remove that discrimination against organized labour. There can be no question that the proposed amend-

ment is in acordance with the views of organized labour in Canada, as the Trades and Labour Congress have made their position clear in this matter. Therefore, I would make an earnest appeal to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State in connection with the proposed legislation, to. alter the act in order that this discrimination may be removed. I know, and all members of the House know, that the Prime Minister is as deeply interested in the affairs of labour as any hon. member in this House, and I am sure, if he were convinced that labour was being discriminated against in this regard, that he, in common with the rest of us, would not hesitate for a single moment to act. I make this appeal to the gentleman who is responsible for the legislation, and to the Prime Minister, because I feel that in so doing we will be working to the best advantage of labour and giving it an opiportunity for the fullest expression of opinion at the polls, an opportunity which perhaps may be otherwise denied. I am not prepared to agree with the remarks of the hon. member for East Galgary, in so far as he seeks to impute any motives to. the government in connection with this matter. I do not want to be put in the position of imputing motives to anybody, and consequently in that spirit of fair play I ask the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State to give labour the benefit of this proposed amendment, and I am sure the result will be to the great advantage of labour and likewise will enure to the great advantage of the community in general.

I think it is not necessary for me
to add very much to what has been said in support of this amendment. We ask only for fair play for labour. I take it that the time has gone by when any hon. member of this House will deny to labour the right, if labour so chooses, to take political action through the formation of its own organizations. We are all familiar with the fact that all over the world to-day there are distinct labour parties. We are all familiar with the record of the labour party in Great Britain. I quite concede that Canada is not industrialized as Great Britain is, but a great many labour men in Canada have come from Great Britain, and they feel they ought to look to Great Britain for a lead along this line. It seems to me that the parliament of Canada would be well advised if they encouraged a movement of this character. Let me point out, as I did in committee, that when this matter was up recently in the British house, and an effort was made to get rid of legisla-

Elections Act
tion which gave an opportunity to Labour people to subscribe funds for election purposes, Mr. Baldwin made one of the most notable speeches of his career in appealing for labour, even against the measure as advanced by his own followers and insisted that labour should have eveiy right to control its own funds.
With regard to a suggestion made by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride), I urge that it would be very unwise indeed to attempt to say just in what manner labour unions should dispose of their funds. They have the right to dispose of their own funds, according to their own regulations. The great evil surrounding the contribution of funds lies in secrecy. In the case of labour unions, before any amount can be voted, the matter is brought before the whole membership in regular business session, and if they choose to support any particular candidate, whether it be the Labour candidate, or the Liberal or Conservative candidate, they are to be at liberty to make their decision.
I would point out also to the government that the Labour party throughout the country is beginning to revise its estimate as to how much it may obtain or hope to obtain through the present administration. We have come here pleading for provision for unemployment, for old age pensions, for the eight hour day, and for active interference in industrial disputes in such a way that the interests of the labour man may be safeguarded. We have had again and again for four years troubles in Nova Scotia, and this government absolutely refuses to take any effective action in regard to safeguarding the interests of .the workers. Again we have to plead that the laws now on the statute book, placed there in 1919, which discriminated against labour by certain clauses in the Immigration Act and in the Criminal Code, should be removed. None of these things has been done. Now we come urging for one little amendment closely connected with the good government of the country. That is something that'will facilitate labour in electing its own representatives.
As I said on a previous occasion, again and again when labour men strike or take some other form of industrial action, gentlemen in all parts of this country protest that labour ought to use parliamentary means, that labour ought to seek to present its case on the floor of the House of Commons or in the various provincial assemblies. Yet, when labour makes any effort whatever to assert its rights by the use of the parliamentary machine, it finds itself effectively blocked. We believe in that 3174
respect there is a distinct discrimination against labour, and we ask in all fairness that this particular clause should be removed.

The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), in introducing this resolution, has stressed the point that he has the support of organized labour. Last week, and again yesterday afternoon, I introduced an amendment to another clause of this bill which would have resulted in prohibiting orientals from voting in British Columbia. That amendment has the sanction of every organized labour body in British Columbia. It has the sanction of all unorganized labour in British Columbia and of a very large proportion of people who are not classified as labour or unorganized labour in that province. But I failed to get any support for that amendment on either of those occasions from the hon gentleman who now threatens us with what organized labour will do or think if we do not, support his amendment. Moreover, when I brought in that amendment, I think it is within the knowledge of the House, I couched it in respectful language as respects the government and as anxious only to see it accepted. I did not challenge the government to reject it nor use offensive language in connection with it. Therefore, I think it would have been more appropriate if the hon. member for East. Calgary had supported that amendment than, for him to ask me to join him now in his wholesale condemnation of the government before he sees what the government are going to do. I would feel inclined to support 'this amendment if it is a thing that will benefit labour, for after all, why should I not do so? I have been a workingman all my life, and I am yet as far as that goes. I would be more willing to do it if I had some assurance that the money so collected from those labour unions would be used for the election of labour representatives in this House who would devote their time and energy to the initiation of really useful constructive legislation- for the benefit of the working men and women of Canada, and not of representatives who indulge in the theoretical shadow-chasing and vague glittering generalities that we have-listened to for the last four years.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
I want to assure the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) that he has come to wrong conclusions in regard to the attitude of the government in reference to not taking any interest in any matters -that he or his. colleagues bring before the House because of their small representation in this chamber. I
Elections Act

know I am voicing the sentiments of all my colleagues and, I believe, of practically every hon. member. Every hon. member has a number of labour organizations and labour men in his constituency, and I feel that these hon. gentlemen have just as much sympathy with labour as have the special representatives who are with us in this chamber to-day. I know, speaking for myself, if I were to err at all, I would rather err in giving consideration to matters suggested by them because of the very fact that they are not as largely represented as other occupations in this country. I think my hon. friend is entirely wrong 12 noon when he charges hon. members of this House with not being sympathetic to any matters that he may bring before this chamber because of the fact that the representation of labour is not large in this House. The main reason why I would beg for nonacceptance of the amendment moved by my hon. friend is this: This matter has been before the House previously on an amendment when the bill was in committee. It was thought by the majority of this House that the amendment at that time would not be acceptable. This bill was before a special committee on Privileges and Elections which gave consideration to it. The amendment was considered here in committee and a vote taken on it, and I believe the consensus of opinion in this chamber was that we should not relax in any way the securities we have in regard to contributions for political purposes. That is all we have in mind in regard to it. It may be that clause 10 would be much improved by this and other amendments, I am not going to discuss this at the present time; but the reason I take the stand of not accepting the amendment moved by my hon. friend is that the matter has been considered in two or three different ways during the present session, and I feel this is not the time to accept it.
Hon. HUGH 'GUTHRIE (South Wellington) : I regret very much I was not present in the House when the amendment introduced by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) was up for consideration. My inclination would have been to support the amendment and to strike out clause 10 or those particular words in clause 10 which restrict political subscriptions to associations or corporations expressly formed for the purpose. To my mind, clause 10 is about the most useless and innocuous clause in the Dominion Elections Act. There is in that clause some language which is also in the act. Those particular words:-" other than a company incorporated for political purposes "-were in-

serted in the act to protect a single political organization, the Ontario Liberal Association, which some twenty-five years ago was incorporated for political purposes. If hon. members will refer to Hansard of about twenty-five years ago and again to Hansard of, I think, the year 1907, to the speech of Sir Allen Aylesworth, then Minister of Justice of Canada, they will see that he specifically preserved the right of the Ontario Liberal Association as an association incorporated for political purposes. When the act was up for revision five years ago, we maintained the section, I think almost in its integrity, but in my humble judgment it has been a useless and innocuous section. There are at the present time in Canada many associations incorporated for political purposes. Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved the second reading of and concurrence in the seventeenth^ amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 70, to amend the Pension Act.
He said:	I wish to make a brief explanation in connection with the action of the Senate in regard to the message which we sent to them a few days ago. The House thought it proper to ask the Senate not to insist upon three different amendments they had made to the pension bill as passed by this House.
. Mr. MACLEAN (York):	Does the minister consider that a money bill? iMr. Lapointe.]

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: PENSION ACT AMENDMENT CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It is not a regular money
bill. A body constituted by parliament has the exclusive power of awarding pensions, and payment can be made by parliament only after such award is made. The Senate have decided not to insist upon two of the three amendments to which I have referred, but to insist upon the amendment they made to the clause regarding appeal. I read in the Montreal Gazette of this morning a report which unwittingly ill-describes the situation. It is represented in that report that the Senate agreed to insist only upon the amendment which it had made to the pension bill prohibiting the granting of pensions in cases where disability was to be traced to misconduct. That is not the situation as it exists. We have never attempted to prohibit payment of pension to men whose disability was to be traced to misconduct. What we attempted to do was to provide an appeal for all those men who on that ground were refused a pension. A decision on the part of the Board of Pension Commissioners not to grant pension on the ground that the disability was due to misconduct is tantamount to saying that the disability was not attributable to war service, and in all other cases where the decision is that the disability was not attributable to war service there is the right of appeal. The Justice department has given the opinion that where the Board of Pension Commissioners decide that the disability was due to misconduct and that therefore no pension can be awarded, there is no appeal, and we had provided in the bill for such an appeal. The Senate has chosen to insist on its amendment. I do not propose to move for a conference at this late hour; I do not think that any useful purpose can be served by it. The Senate acted in full cognizance of the whole situation and circumstances. I can only express regret that at least for a few months more the men who have been turned down on this ground and who feel that they have been unfairly dealt with will be precluded from entering an appeal.
Motion agreed to; amendment read the second time and concurred in.

This bill has been requested by representatives of the civil service. Under the Superannuation Act of last year they were given until the 19th of July of this year to elect whether or not they would come under that act. They now ask that the time be extended for another year, and all we are doing is to substitute "two years" for "one year". The bill is introduced to meet their wishes. I am not pressing it* if there is any objection.
That is not a very illuminating attitude-

Perhaps the discussion

On section 1

Time of election extended.

I have no further explanation
to offer than that already given. This is to extend the time of election for another year. I brought in the bill at the request of representatives of the civil service. I admit they should have already elected whether they would come under this act or not, but perhaps it is not unreasonable to give them another year.

What are the reasons
they advance? If the minister has none of his own, perhaps he would pass on their reasons.

Perhaps I might be allowed to give an illustration. Take the case of a man sixty or sixty-five years of age who will within a very short time be retired. He has paid into the retirement fund, under the previous regulations, a considerable amount of money, which he would be allowed to draw out in a lump sum on his retirement unless he elected to come under the new Superannuation Act. A number of them have not yet elected whether or not they will relinquish their grasp on. that lump sum they can withdraw under the old scheme and let it go into the new superannuation fund, as it would have to do if they elected to come under that scheme. Some of the employees in that class desire a little longer time in which to decide whether to draw out the amount to their credit in the retirement fund, or to relinquish that and take advantage of the benefits that would accrue to them under the Superannuation Act that was passed last year.

This makes clear the
advantages of waiting, I know, but then a time limit has been fixed. Do they give any reason why they should have another year, and if so, what is the reason?

The only reason is the
uncertainty which some of them are in as to which course it would be advisable for them to take, whether to get their money in a lump sum, and in some cases it amounts to two or three thousand dollars, and be done with all superannuation schemes, or to come in under the new act. It is just a question of uncertainty in the minds of some of them as to which course they should take.

Catching the contagion
of the government, and falling into ways of procrastination.

I think also some question
has arisen as to the interpretation of various sections of the Superannuation Act. I know that in some civil service organizations with which I am familiar these questions have arisen, and they have asked for another year in which to elect, pending assurances as to the real interpretation of the act.

I would ask the
minister if this act would cover the cases of some seven or eight guards or more in the penitentiary who would have to pay into the superannuation fund a large sum of money in order to get the benefits of this act. The officials who have been there for twenty-odd years have not the amount of money that it is necessary to pay into the new superannuation fund in order to bring them under the
Superannuation Act

act. At the same time, they have laid up a gratuity in some cases of some two thousand dollars or more, which would come to them, in case of resignation from the service. Now these few officials would like some change in the Superannuation Act, so that instead of paying in the lump sum that is required to come in under the new act, they shall be credited with die amount that has accumulated to their credit after twenty-five or twenty-six years service. They are withheld from entering into the superanuuation scheme on account of the large amount of money, some $1,500, which they would have to pay in in a lump sum to come under the scheme. I would like to ask the minister in charge or the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Labour if their case will be considered, and an amendment made to the act so as to permit of some change being made in their case.

This amendment does not
change their status in any way. It does not in any way change the Superannuation Act, except as to extending the time of election. I know there have been representations made to us from various sources to widen the act, but we have refused to meddle with it at all. We propose to let it have another year's operation.

Might I ask the
Minister of Labour or the Minister of Justice to make some statement that the cases of these men will be considered? I think they will agree with me that it is impossible for these men to pay in that lump sum of money.

There are a considerable number of employees in the service in somewhat the same position. For instance, down at the Printing Bureau we have several hundred employees who are not now under this Superannuation Act that was passed last year, whereas they were under the Calder Act, which expired last year. That situation and a number of similar situations possibly should be dealt with by parliament at some time, but this amendment does not change the situation at all in relation to the employees my hon. friend speaks about, except to give them one year longer in order to elect which they shall do.

May I point out
that in the meantime these employees are taking great chances. There is a ease now, and it will come up in the supplementary estimates, of an employee with about twenty-six years' service who became sick. If he had been informed that he was going to die within a very short time, he could have resigned, but he died and he lost his $1,800. He was not 
under the Superannuation Act. A number of these sad cases may arise, and I think the minister would be doing a very creditable thing if he would assure us that their case will receive immediate consideration. I shall have something further to say on this matter when the estimates come up.

I would not advise the

Take the one clause which provides that mortgages under this legislation shall take precedence over all taxes,-school taxes, municipal taxes, and every other lien and charge. Does the minister imagine that any municipality or province could possibly permit such a thing as that? Why, you could not conduct your school system under such circumstances. Even to-day there are many scores of school districts which cannot sustain themselves, and the fact that our soldier settlement lands that have fallen into the hands of the government are exempt has been a contributory cause.
I am not attributing any fault to the government in that respect because it is difficult to take the stand that these lands should be taxable. But for goodness' sake do not suggest that we go further. There is not the slightest chance in the world of any government permitting mortgages under this legislation to take precedence of school taxes. How could the school district ever protect itself against the mortgagor? How could it

Rural Credits
protect its security? Here they have a lien on land, a mortgage against it, with a mortgage sale proceeding started. How will they protect their lien? They have three or four hundred dollars in accrued taxes and they have no power to bid in the mortgage; and what is more, they never could provide the money if they had the power. Six Nations Indians who

The department, I believe, hold in trust certain funds accumulated by the sale of property which belonged to the Indians when they were first given their grant in Canada. I am sorry to say-of course the department understands the situation more fully than I do- there is a feeling on the reserve in regard to certain things which the department has done. A year or two ago the department abolished .the	old	hereditary council	and
established a new system of electing the council. I do not know that this has worked out altogether satisfactorily, but I do not want to press that at all to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The hon.
member resides beside the reserve. Does he not think the	new	system	of election	has
improved the situation somewhat?

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I think it would have been
a wise thing if the 'band themselves had had an opportunity of having some kind of referendum to say which system they preferred. I believe I can safely say that the majority of the band to-day are not in favour of the elective system.	It	is very	hard to get	theIndians to take	any	part in	an election	or a
referendum.

I should like to mention one or two matters to the minister and see if possibly some consideration cannot .be given to them by the department. The first question I want to ask is about the secretary of the old hereditary council, Mr. Hill. He was regularly appointed and he resided on the reserve for some length of time. All communications from the department went to him. in fact, I think up to the time when the old hereditary council was abolished. During the last two or three years of his incumbency he has not been paid his salary. I do not think the secretary should be penalized in any way on account of any disagreement between the department and the council, because the secretary, after all, holds a secretarial position and is not responsible for the' action of the council. I would urge upon the department that Mr. Hill should be paid his salary. I understand the interest from their trust funds is used largely for educational purposes and for the maintenance of roads and bridges. Perhaps the minister will state whether this is so. I should also like to know if the schools on the reserve are conducted according to the provincial regulations requiring properly qualified teachers. I see that in one of the Auditor General's reports there is an entry of bonus payments to these teachers. What is this bonus given for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The school
regulations are much the same as those governing public schools of the province in which the reserve may be located. The bonus referred to is the cost of living bonus. Although this is one of the finest of our Indian reserves, there has been a rather bitter fight there for a number of years between two factions on almost everything relating to the administration of the reserve, including the old system under which they selected their councillors on an hereditary basis. We thought it well to widen the selection by changing the system to an elective basis. Naturally when a drastic change of this kind is made resentment will be aroused, but I do not think we could have allowed the hereditary council to function very much longer on account of the arbitrary manner in which it wa3 treating the people. As to the salary owing to David Hill, he was appointed by the old council, without reference to the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs at all, and he carried on very arbitrarily, refusing to make returns to the department, and so far we have no returns of the transactions of the council for that particular period. We have no desire to keep Mr. Hill out of his money, but we do insist on getting those returns. It may

Supply-Indian Affairs
be somewhat unfair to penalize him for the shortcomings of the council, but we feel that he could, if he so desired, get us all the information we are entitled to.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Of course, I realize that there
have been differences between the department and the old council, but I must repeat that I do not think Mr. Hill should be penalized for the failure of the council to make proper returns. As to the change made by the minister from an hereditary to an elective council, it must not be forgotten that the Six Nations Indians are in rather a unique position. They came to Canada from the United States at the time of the American Revolution and were given their reserve by the British crown. Although the Haldimand Treaty possibly did not make any specific reference to the rights of the Indians with respect to administration, it is generally conceded that they were to be allowed to look after their own municipal affairs. That privilege is gradually being taken away from them, and I think it is the main cause of the longstanding differences between the band and the department. I would urge that the minister should give further consideration to Mr. Hill's claim, and I think it is very unjust that it has been neglected so long.
I understand that the band has been asked to ratify a certain oil lease which the department proposes to grant to a certain company. The lease, as I understand it, will tie up all the land of the reserve and will effectually prevent any individual Indians making arrangements whereby they would have the privilege of enjoying free gas or oil. Therefore it seems to me that the proposal is not in the best interests of the whole band.

speechtext:
I had the advantage of
listening to a delegation representing this land some time ago. They presented their case with really remarkable ability and a native eloquence that was inspiring. I presume the minister has had some experience of that kind. They made serious indictments against the department, but the gist of it all was the lack
Supply-Indian Affairs

of fairness and frankness in dealing with them. They claimed-and they seemed to have evidence to support the claim-that those supporting the hereditary system were not given a hearing before the commissioner who investigated, or was supposed to investigate, their difficulties; that they were treated rather cavalierly, and their secretary has been denied his remuneration. They also made a complaint, which I recall very well, with respect to the type of teacher, in both spheres, sent to instruct them. I must say they presented their case about as ably as any I have ever heard by way of delegation, and I am sure the member for the riding, who knows more about the band than any other hon. member is voicing the sentiments of the people in that district when he expresses some sympathy with these Indians. This tribe, I think, deserve better of us than any other in Canada; certainly no other deserves more than does the Six Nations Indian tribe. They came here in the capacity of United Empire Loyalists. They left their own country and came to stand by the British flag in these dominions, and they came under certain treaty rights which we should' scrupulously and sacredly honour and protect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I entirely
agree with my right hon. friend as to the manner in which the Indians can present their claims. Indeed, for a year and a half after I took charge of the Indian department I thought they were the most abused people on the face of the earth, from the representations they made to me; but I discovered on closer acquaintance with them that they were very adroit at presenting their case. I have gone to Brantford on three occasions and consulted with the member for that riding (Mr. Raymond) as well as many other prominent people in the locality. The agent who was then in charge, and who has since died, had perhaps the most troublous and turbulent time of any agent in the employ of the government. He was a very decent chap, but all hon. members will agree with me, I think, when I say that he had a very troublous time. Evictions were being made and the people of the reserve were being treated in the most arbitrary manner. In fact, so bad did the conditions become that we had to ask that a detachment of police be placed upon the reserve; It was quite out of the question to permit that sort of thing to go on; we had to call a halt. In addition, there was a chief by the name of Deskaheh who finally appeared at the League of Nations to lay his troubles before that body. He had to leave the country, and he was aided and

abetted by an American lawyer. His argument, of course, was that these Indians were British subjects; that they were not amenable to the laws of Canada but 'were allies of the British. Now, I have no quarrel with that sort of thing, but it must be borne in mind that there are two elements on that reserve, the Christian element and the pagan element, between whom the feeling existing is not of the best and it is a little difficult to stand in between those two elements and preserve order. But I notice that since the inauguration of the elective system they have not had nearly so much trouble. I will say for David Hill that he is one of the cleverest platform speakers I have listened to, and he can make a presentation of a case that is somewhat difficult to refute. I know all these gentlemen very well; I have had three years' acquaintance with them. But I wish the committee to believe that the difficulties are not by any means all on one side. I will say that if there are difficulties now I am not hearing so much about them as I did formerly. The people are living in peace and quiet, something that they were unable to do prior to the inauguration of the new system.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I would not like the minister to give the committee the impression that under present conditions the situation is all that could be desired. One section of the tribe, which is in the vast majority so far as numbers go, are doing their best to keep the peace and to obey the law and they are accepting the present situation in the best possible spirit. On the other hand, I would like to plead with the minister and with the department for the adoption of a little more conciliatory attitude, because these men, after all, have their grievances. I live close to them myself, I have talked with a good many of them, and I know their attitude. I know they are loyal to the British Crown, and their grievances are only over such small differences as occur in local administration. Possibly it would not be wise for me to say anything more, but in closing I just want to plead with the minister once more to adopt a conciliatory attitude so far as the department is concerned, and I think it would be in the interests of the department itself to settle these few small matters.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I wish to bring before the
committee a petition which I presented to this House on June 15th from the Peigan Indian Band, praying for the cancellation of a certain lease granted to the Hon. A. J. McLean, covering a large portion of their reserve-although a majority of the Indians had voted against the lease. I regret, Mr. Chairman, that I should have to delay the committee this afternoon when we are so near
prorogation, and I presume a great many members will be rather impatient that this matter should be taken up to-day, but I do hot think it is my fault in any way. I would like to have discussed it on previous occasions, but I have deferred doing so to suit the convenience of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and I think his convenience should be considered before that of private members.
The Indians in their petition ask for the cancellation of this lease on the ground that they were assured by Commissioner Laird, who negotiated the treaty with them in 1877. that their reserve would not be occupied without their consent. I wish to quote very briefly the words used by Commissioner Laird when he negotiated this treaty with the Indians. I am quoting from a book "Treaties of Canada with the Indians of the Northwest" by Morris. The Hon. Mr. Morris was at one time Lieutenant Governor of the Northwest Territories, and is, I think, very well qualified to speak on all Indian affairs. He sets out in this book the reasons why the government of Canada were very anxious to negotiate this treaty with the Indians. Briefly, the reason was that the Indians, who held a natural title, as he states, to this land, were anxious that the treaty should be negotiated, and the government were anxious also because many white settlers were desirous of securing homesteads in that part of the country. The treaty was negotiated by the Hon. David Laird and Colonel McLeod of the Northwest Mounted Police. In order not to take up too much time, I will quote briefly from Commissioner Laird, who, at page 257 of this book, says in regard to this treaty:
On Tuesday we met the Indians at the usual hour. We further explained the terms outlined to them yesterday, dwelling especially upon the fact that by the Canadian law their reserves could not be taken from them, occupied or sold without their consent.
I would ask the House whether a lease for ten years means occupation or not.
The late Colonel McLeod is quoted -at page 275 as saying to the Indians:
You say that I have always kept my promises. As surely as my past promises have been kept, so surely shall those made by the Commissioners be carried out in the future. If they were broken I would be ashamed to meet you or look you in the face; but every promise will be solemnly fulfilled as certainly as the sun now shines down upon us from the heavens. I shall always remember the kind manner in which you have to-day spoken of me.
After this there was a great shaking of hands and the council ended. The late Colonel McLeod, who afterwards became chief justice of Alberta has gone, and the present Super-
49S4
Supply-Indian Affairs

intendent General of Indian Affairs, in spite of these promises that were made to the Indians at that time, has against the vote of the band leased a large part of this reserve. There are many quotations given here by the late Lieutenant Governor Morris along similar lines but I think the two I have quoted should be enough to show the House the nature of the promises made to the Indians by the two commissioners on that occasion.
Section 40 of the Indian Act provides that no leases of any Indian land shall be granted without the consent of the band, and that a vote shall be taken, and a record of the vote kept in the Indian office. When I discussed this matter in the House last year, the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs stated that he understood the Indians had voted in favour of this lease. On the 8th of July last he made the following statement, as will be seen at page 4332 of Unrevised Hansard, July 8, 1924:
We never lease land on an Indian reserve unless the band has voted in favour of it, which vote is registered in our office.
This shows clearly that the practice of the department in the past has always been to obtain the consent of the band. I find that an attempt was made to secure consent to this lease. A year ago I asked for a return of all correspondence passing between the government and any other parties in connection with this lease. This return when brought down contained a letter from the Indian Commissioner dated April 2 in which he states very clearly that an effort had been made to secure the consent of the Indians. He said:
With regard to the Peigan lease, I gave the Ind.ian Agent, Mr. Arthur, strict instructions to negotiate with the Indians for the surrender of 30,000 acres of grazing to be leased to Mr. McLean. The whole matter was fully discussed with them by the agent. They could not come to an agreement. I then sent one of the inspectors up from this office to see the Indians, and he was not successful in getting a surrender for leasing.
On my return to Alberta last year the Indians asked me to come to Macleod to see them in connection with this lease and while I was there the Indian Chief requested me to interview their lawyer in company with himself. From my conversation with Mr. Fawcett I learned that certain correspondence passing between himself and the Department had not been included in the return brought down. This year when I came back to Ottawa I asked the Deputy Superintendent General if there was such correspondence in the department and he later on brought down a supplementary return. This return I
[Mr. Coote.l
have in my hand and it shows that three or four letters were written by Mr. Fawcett who was at that time, I think, mayor of Macleod. The letters are addressed to the Superintendent General protesting against this lease, on behalf of the Indians. The first letter dated January 9 includes a petition signed by some seventy of the male members of the band protesting against the lease being granted. There follows a reply from the Superintendent General, with a further letter from Mr. Fawcett dated January 31, 1924. In this letter Mr. Fawcett points out that the Indians claim that the granting of the lease would be a violation of the treaty which was entered into with them by the Hon. David Laird and Colonel McLeod on behalf of the government of Canada. They also point out that only fourteen Indians had voted in favour of the lease. Mr. Fawcett in this letter says:
Surely the department will not arbitrarily ignore the treaty with the Indians and lease their land without their consent.
I want to quote the reply of the Superintendent General under date February 16, 1924, to Mr. Fawcett:
As you are probably aware, the Indian Act gives the department authority to take whatever action it deems to be in the best interests of the Indians; and as the Indians are costing the people of Canada a considerable amount annually, it becomes necessary from time to time to take such action as is in their best interests, at the same time relieving the taxpayers of Canada to this extent.
This is -the question I want to ask the Superintendent General and the members of this committee: For the paltry sum of $1,300 odd should we sacrifice Canada's good name by a violation of a treaty with the Indians, when we spend $1,400 to erect a flagpole on pur magnificent new parliament building?

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: How much does the hon. member think our good name is worth?

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I think it is worth considerably more than that.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
And it is getting to be
of greater value every day.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
If the taxpayers of Canada
were consulted in regard to this small sum which we are receiving for this lease they would say that the lease should be cancelled and that Canada's obligations under this treaty should be considered as something more than a scrap of paper. In order that those who care to read this debate may be fully informed in regard to this matter, I should like with the permission of the House to put these letters on Hansard. They are

Supply-Indian Affairs
not very long and they form a part of the supplementary return brought down this year.
Macleod, Alberta,
January 9, 1924.
Superintendent,
Indian Affairs,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Peigan Reserve Lease
Dear Sir,-I enclose you herewith list of negative votes in connection with the proposed lease to Archie McLean of some thirty-seven or more Sections at 6 cents an acre which the Indians stated to me he would fence if granted the lease. This document was brought into me by Philip Big Swan, Head Chief, Leo Smith, Minor chief and Percy Smith, cousin of the Minor chief.
These men pointed out that it is not satisfactory to have any of the reserve leased. Years ago Maun-sell Brothers had a lease, and that the pasturing and the opportunity to cut hay gradually grew less and during the years of 17-18 and 19 the Indians were not able to put up hay sufficient for their stock, resulting in the winter of 1920 in a tremendous loss of stock and a very large expense of money and labour to purchase hay for the stock on the reserve. Since that time the stock has been increasing and these men state that if a large portion of the reserve is leased they will find themselves in exactly the same position as obtained a few years ago when the range was heavily pastured by Maunsell Brothers. They point out further that in fencing thirty-seven sections a very large portion of the best watering places will be enclosed by the fences and the Indian stock forced to w'ater elsewhere.
It would seem that this application to lease and the advisability of it was not discussed with the Chiefs of the reserve. May I point out that the Head Chief and two minor chiefs Leo Smith and Many Chief, are against the lease, sixty-five I believe in all.
Kindly give this matter your usual good attention in the best interests of these Indian Wards.
Yours truly,
John L. Fawcett.
Macleod, Alberta, January, 31, 1924.
Honourable Charles Stewart,
Superintendent of Indian Affairs,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Peigan Reserve Lease
Dear Sir,-Your favour of the 19th inst., at hand and contents carefully noted.
Philip Big Swan, the head chief came in again to-day and expressed himself and the other Indians who are with him very strongly in the matter. He asked me to point out to you with the other Indians the action of the Department in going ahead to lease the reserve, was a complete renunciation of their treaty which their fathers had made in years gone by when it was agreed that the Indians should have this land so long as the grass grew and the river ran. He tells me that w'hen they talked the matter over at the agency at Brocket, only four Indians were in favour of leasing, and all those whose names I sent you were against it, but Philip Big Swan tells me that he thinks some ten people signed it before that. He further tells me that there has never been on the reserve any notice sent around and the day fixed when all the male Indians over twenty-one years could go in and vote for the leasing or against it.
It is very apparent that if all the male Indians were asked their opinion the big majority would be against leasing and if this is so surely the Department will not arbitrarily ignore the treaty with these Indians and lease their land without their consent.
It might not be so bad if all the chiefs were in favour, but the fact is, the Head Chief, Philip Big Swan, and the minor chiefs, Leo Smith, Many Chiefs. Man Who Smokes are all against it and the fifth chief, Crow Eagle was away at the time they had their talk at Brocket, but he is probably against it. Thus, yon have a great many of the Indians against it and all of the Chiefs but one and probably all of them, and yet the department in the face of that seem to intend to follow Commissioner Graham's recommendation. Thi3 surely is a very serious way of dealing with the management of the reserve.
Since I last wrote, the Chief informs me that an Inspector Christenson from Regina has been up to ses them and knows now that very many of the Indians are against the leasing and he told the Chief that he would report the matter to Commissioner Graham. At the same time the Chief and other Indians explained personally why they did not want the lease.
Kindly bear in mind that the representation as I have made as above has been given me direct by the Indians themselves and are only -worded as best I could to express their position.
I am not personally interested but I cannot refrain from saying that I have known the Head Chief for quite a number of years and his conception of what is best for the Indians on the Reserve should be given great respect for he is shrewd and reliable.
Yours truly,
Jno. L. Fawcett.
Ottawa, Ontario,
February 16, 1924.
Dear Mr. Fawcett,
I have your favour of the 31st ultimo re the Peigan Reserve lease.
As you are probably aware, the Indian Act gives the Department authority to take whatever action it deems to be in the best interests of the Indians; and as the Indians are costing the people of Canada a considerable amount annually, it becomes necessary, from time to time, to take such action as is in their best interests, at the same time relieving the taxpayers of Canada to this extent.
In the present case,t the necessary pasturage is available and the department has concluded that it is in the interests of the Indians to execute the lease.
Yours faithfully,
Charles Stewart.
His Worship Mayor Fawcett, LL.B.,
Macleod, Alberta.
John L. Fawcett, LL.B.
Barrister, Notary Public, etc.,
Macleod, Alta.
March 6, 1924.
Superintendent General,
Indian Affairs,
Ottawa, Ontario.

Dear Sir:
Your favour of 16th ultimo was duly submittted *o the Head Chief of the Reserve and he in turn took the matter up with the Minor Chief and the other Indians and they returned to-day asking me to write j'ou further, pointing out to you as follows:-
They signed the original petition because they believe there is not sufficient pasture and hay available and further that some of the land to be included in the lease has Indian settlers thereon.

They note what you say in regard to the Indians costing the people of Canada large sums of money and they answer that the Treaty which they signed by their now dead Chiefs arranged for that and they were promised that they would be looked after.

has not settled or cleaned up the former.
They complain that it looks to them as though the Government was not trying very hard to take care of, their interests, that surely the Head Indians of the tribe ought to be considered as having some knowledge as to what is in their interest.
Only a short time ago they agreed to sell a small portion of the Reserve for the Lethbridge Northern Right of way and that this money has been duly received and distributed and they fail to understand why the Dominion Government does not deal the same way with the people under its particular care.

Brocket', Alta.,
April 4, 1924.
Rt. Hon. M. King,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-We respectfully submit to your Excellency that we members of the Peigan Band of Indians do express our disappointment of a certain lease, which we have learnt from Commissioner Graham, that Hon. Chas. Stewart has granted to Mr. A. McLean.
A meeting was called for by Indian Agent Mr. C. A. Arthur, a vote took place, a majority of over three-quarters of the voters was against the said lease.
Experience has taught us to do away with such leases. We have leased our reserve for the past twenty years to Maunsell Bros., and we know the consequences. We never received a cent of the lease money and then the dry years came so our stock had to die.
We understand it will be a closed lease not in one block, but in three parts, twenty-four sections, ten section in another, and three sections, so it will take up the best grazing land we have, including the springs and watering places, when it is fenced our stock at large will suffer for want of water.
We surrendered thirty-six sections of our reserve, about thirty-six sections is fenced in for farming purposes and Mr. McLean got on or about thirty-seven sections.
We have about 2,800 head of stock, cattle and horses, to graze the balance of our reserve. If we should get dry years again and do not save our grass now our stock will die on us again. So we think we will be far better off to not have the lease, six cents an acre or three dollars and twenty cents for each Indian is not enough.
This lease is against the Indians' will, and so we are asking you for protection, to see into the matter and to find out why should they force this lease on us. An answer will oblige.
We are, Sir,
Yours obediently,
Jno. Crow Eagle, M.C.
I also obtained from the department this year a record of the vote taken in connection with this lease. I find that was taken on January 7, 1924 under the superintendence of Mr. C. A. Arthur, the Indian Agent. Seventeen Indians voted in favour of the lease and fifty-three against. I am giving these particulars in view of the statement made last year by the Superintendent General to the effect that he understood that the Indians had voted in favour of the lease. I have also a letter from the Indian Commissioner in which he states very plainly that the Indians voted against the granting of the lease and the matter was reported on by him to the minister. The commissioner apparently could not have advised the minister to that effect; Mr. Fawcett of Macleod states very clearly in his letters that the Indians were opposed to the lease. In view of that fact I think I am fully justified in suggesting to the minister that the lease should now be cancelled. I would point out to the committee before leaving this phase of the question that on April 4 one of the chiefs of this band, John Crow Eagle, addressed a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) protesting against the lease and stating that a large majori:y of the Indians had voted against it. This letter was forwarded to the Indian department for a reply to the Indian chief; it was forwarded by the department at Ottawa to the Indian Commissioner at Regina, and the Indian chief was finally answered by the commissioner. I desire the permission of the committee to place on Hansard this one letter from the Indian chief.
I have brought this matter up here because the Indians said to me, "We feel that we have no one to speak for us. When we try to talk to Ottawa it is like talking through a ten-foot wall, and we hope you will take the matter up for us there and see if parliament will not restore to us our treaty rights." One old Indian chief said to me, "Will you tell the members at Ottawa that' we think they are wise men, and if they are wise men they will surely say that the treaty with the Indians should not be broken. I would like every member of this House to consider that statement of the old Indian chief. In 1918 the Indian Act was amended by adding subsection 3 to section 90, which gives the Superintendent General power under certain circumstances to lease the Indian lands without 'a surrender, and it seems to me that it could only be under the authority given here that a lease could be granted to Mr. McLean when the Indians had voted against the lease. I ask the House to note that

Supply-Indian Affairs
this power is to be used only in case the Indians are neglecting or refusing to cultivate or make use of the land, and I do not think it can be' shown that the Indians were either refusing or neglecting to make use of the land in question. I wish I could show to hon. members a map of this Peigan reserve. It would show that the lease granted to Mr. McLean covers three distinct and separate parts of the reserve, about 5,000 acres in the northeast corner, 15,000 acres in the southeast comer and approximately 1.900 acres in the southwest corner, and covers. altogether 22,560 acres. The original area of this reserve was 116,000 acres, but the Indians surrendered for sale in 1919, 22,000 acres, and there has been surrendered, for railway right of way 775 acres, leaving the Indians now 92,000 acres. From that 22,000 acres has been'leased, which leaves the Indians a total of 70,000 acres. As I have already pointed out, the lease covers three separate portions of the reserve. The small part of three sections in the southwest comer of this reserve was a part of the Indian stock farm, and Mr. McLean secured this part, without having to put up any fence at all. The northeast corner of the reserve, where Mr. McLean has about 5,000 acres, the Indians have always used for a winter pasture. The reserve is divided almost equally into two parts by the Canadian Pacific Railway and Old Man river, running diagonally across the reserve. The Indian homes are nearly all on the north side of the railway. The Indians took their cattle over to the north side of the railway in the wintertime, and in the past they have always used a portion of the northeast corner of the reserve for a winter pasture. Under the terms of this lease Mr. McLean has secured practically all of this corner of the reserve and he has fenced this part of his lease thus shutting out the Indian cattle from their winter pasture. This winter a large number of the Indian cattle when turned out drifted down the long narrow strip of land which was left between the railway right of way and Mr. McLean's fence, and a great number of them drifted off the reserve. The Indian chief told me that Mr. McLean and his man, the Indian chief, and the stock man on the reserve spent over a day gathering cattle and placing them across on the north side of the river. The Indians claimed that if they had had a hard winter this year many of their cattle would have died because they would have had no winter pasture for them. Not only did the Indians use this for a winter pasture, but I find that an Indian widow and her son had their home within the part fenced off by Mr. McLean. I would like 318
to read to the House a letter which I have received from this widow dated April 20, and reads in part:
Then Mr. Webb, a Mounted Police came in and he repeated the same old story to me. He claims that the Indian agent told him to come down to my house and order me out of the leased land, and he also suggested to me that the department wrote to the Indian agent for me to move away from my land.
My answer to Mr. Webb was, "I am not willing to move away, this is my house and I have been living here for last fourteen years. The lease is not granted by the Peigan Indian Act". After all this Mr. Weeb told me to write to the department and make the following statement, so that I will know from the department if it is so that I have to move away or not.
The police told me that he will give me three weeks from the said date to move away.
I want to point out that this is the result of leasing land against the vote of the Indians. I think it is a shame in this country when we come to the point where the mounted police are used by the Indian agent to force Indian widows off their land. I took this letter to the Superintendent General and he was good enough to wire instructions to the Indian agent at Brocket, that this woman was not to be disturbed in possession of her property at the present time. But I also desire to point out that so long as this lease is persisted in this widow is liable to this kind of persecution. I have in my hand a statement given to me by the son of this widow when I was in Macleod last winter. This Indian cannot write English, but this is his story as near as I could put it on paper:
This Indian lives with his mother, the widow of Seth Plain Eagle. His mother has lived in their present location for fourteen years. Their buildings and little farm are included in the part of the lease which Mr. McLean has fenced.
Some time last summer he was given a cheque for .$40.00 by the Indian Agent to pay him for his oats and pasture fence. The Agent also offered his mother $70.00 to move out of her home. He was out haying last summer and fall, living in a tent, and he states that he was told by the Agent that he must not go back to their old home, although he was living there when Mr. McLean put up his fence.
His mother is very anxious to stay at her present home. She has a house, root-house and a log stable, for which she has been offered 170.00, but she has refused to accept this amount.
At the time this statement	was made, these	peoplewere still living in a	tent, as they	were afraid	to go
back to their home. The weather shortly before had been very severe, the temperature being about forty below zero.
This Indian asked me whether I thought he could .go back to his home, and I told him I certainly thought he could in spite of the Indian agent. Under our treaty with the Indians we promised to send them agents to advise and protect them against unscrupulous white men,	but I	am	afraid in	somecases the Indian	agent	has	only delivered
them into the hands of unscrupulous white

Supply-Indian Affairs

men. I should like to emphasize ait this point that, in face of the statement which I have made and which, I think, cannot be disputed, in regard to this part of the reserve which has been used by the Indians for a winter pasture, I do not think it can 'be contended in any court of law that the Indians were neglecting or refusing to use the land, particularly as a widow and her son were living in that area. In addition to that, there are ten or twelve families living on the southeast side of the river within a very few rods, in some cases, of this fence, who used this particular piece of land all the time for their pasture. They are now shut in a narrow strip of land between Mr. McLean's fence and the river. It is no wonder that these people feel very keenly about this lease being granted and insist upon their rights being restored to them.
