maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
One other reason why the
Indians object so strongly to this lease is because of a very unfortunate experience which they had under a lease some years ago which had been given to Mr. Maunsell. That lease ran for a period of seventeen years from 1902 to 1919. During this time Mr. Maunsell ran as many as 2,000 head of cattle, possibly more, over the reserve. I have been unable to secure definite information on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext: About 2,500.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
So many cattle were grazed
on the reserve that during the dry years of 1918 and 1919 the pasture was completely eaten off and the Indians were not able to put up any hay on this reserve, with the result that they were compelled to sell a large number of the Indian cattle. They also spent a large sum of money for feed. They incurred expense putting up hay on the Hobema reserve and shipping it to this reserve. Although they received from Mr. Maunsell in those seventeen years only $19,991, they paid out for feed in the winter of 1919, $13,480, and in the winter of 1920, $30,126, or a total of $42,606. I cannot help thinking that if the reserve had been kept for the Indians, instead of Mr. Maunsell being allowed to have all those cattle on it, sufficient hay could be put up on the reserve to take care of the Indian cattle. One of the most unfortunate , features about their experience was that in 1920 they lost, apparently from starvation,

475 head of cattle. There were on the reserve at the end of the fiscal year 1920, 1.610 head of cattle. At the end of the following year there were only 968, leaving 642 to be accounted for. There were 78 sold during that year and a total killed of 89, leaving, as I have already said, 475 unaccounted for, which apparently died of starvation. In view of the very unfortunate experience which these Indians had under the Maunsell lease, surely the members of this committee and the Superintendent General cannot wonder that the Peigan Indians voted against giving a lease of 22,000 acres to Mr. McLean. I should like you to imagine the feeling of the Indians after this unfortunate experience, to see this lease granted against their wishes. If it were not for taking up so much time, I should like to give the committee the statements that several Indians gave me in regard to this matter, but I am going to forbear. [DOT] I should like to give the committee the statements of the head chief, Big Swan. He said that prior to this hard winter he had 300 head of cattle o? his own. He sold 75 head and he paid out $2,000 himself for feed, and that after the winter was over he had 75 head of cattle left. His stock has now increased to 175, and I should like the committee to imagine the feelings of this Indian chief this winter when he finds the winter pasture fenced off and he is not allowed to pasture his cattle on Indian land. As long as this lease is persisted in, I am afraid the Indians will not be given a fair chance. I am informed that many of the Indian cows have been killed this year for beef, although there were plenty of steers on the reserve. I have also been informed lately that the agent has speved some of the Indian heifers, apparently with the idea of keeping down the number of stock which the Indians have, so that he will be justified in recommending the lease to Mr. McLean.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS

Where did
my hon. friend get that information?

reserve. This is only information which has come to me. I should like the Superintendent General to ask the Indian agent for an affidavit as to whether he has speyed Indian heifers or not. My reason for not giving the names is that the Indians say: We are at the mercy of the Indian agent, and if we write you and give our names, you can easily see that we are liable to persecution by the agent. I was told that the statement was in a Calgary paper that the Indian Comimis-

Supply-Indian Affairs
sioner had said that he was going to try to ship some of the Indian riding ponies east to sell them because of lack of feeding ground.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Not the
ponies on that reserve or near it.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
' Before I leave this phase of the matter, I should like to suggest to the Superintendent General that what he should d.o for the Peigan reserve is to purchase some more cattle for the Indians. The Peigan Indians have a band fund of over $100,000, and if there is room for more cattle on the reserve, the cattle should belong to the Indians and not to outside parties. One other reason I would advance why in my opinion this lease is not in the interests of the Indians is that it is for a term of ten years at a rental of only six cents per acre. I am confident that if leased by public tender the land would bring three or four times the amount, and I have been assured by ranchers living in the vicinity that it is easily worth the higher figure. Under our homestead regulations, a man proving up a homestead with cattle must have at least sixteen head after the second year, or ten acres to each animal. On the same basis it will be found that Mr. McLean will be pasturing his cattle for sixty cents per head per annum. I think that is a pretty nice snap for the man who holds the lease. Under these circumstances. I do not see how the lease can be held to be in the interests of the Indians; and if it is not in their interests, I fail to see why it should ever have been granted.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have tried to cover the ground as quickly as possible, but before concluding I wish to give to the committee a few brief quotations from certain of our prominent public men with respect to the spirit in which we should regard our treaty obligations. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in referring to^ a statement made by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr Woodsworth) thus expressed himself on February 18, 1925:
I heard an hon. member say the other day, speaking, I believe, of the suggested law concerning the eight-hour day, and evidently being impatient of the obstacle put in the way of that enactment in the difficulty of knowing the respective fields of jurisdiction on the part of the Dominion and the provinces-I heard him say, "Well, where there is a will there is a way." I was surprised at that statement. That was the spirit which inspired the invaders of Belgium in 1914, and the world was precipitated in a sea of blood. Surely the British North America Act cannot be made a scrap of paper-
' The CHAIRMAN: Will the hon. member indicate how that quotation is relevant to this item?
318i

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. The treaty I have been speaking about wTas made between Canada and the Indians; that treaty,
I submit, has been violated by the action of the Superintendent General in granting this lease, and therefore it seems to me that the remarks I am quoting are strictly applicable.

speechtext:
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. One of the Indians of the Peigan band, a returned man who fought in France, wrote a letter to the Calgary Herald on this subject, and I quote a dozen lines from it:
These Indian reserves were set aside for us by our representatives in 1877, forever, and that treaty should be held just as sacred as the treaty which made us send our sons to a foreign soil to help fight one of the biggest and best-equipped war machines that ever infested Europe. Former Canadian premiers have always impressed on the minds of the Indians that these reserves were the property of the Indians, and that they cannot be sold or occupied without the Indians' consent.
I have several other quotations from letters written by Indians, but I will forbear reading them lest you might wish to rule me out of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I do not wish to rule
the hon. member out of order, but general statements of the type he quoted first are not considered in Supply as being relevant. This has always been the practice. The last quotation read was directly applicable to the vote.

speechtext:
The Calgary Herald last
winter-I have not the exact date-contained an editorial, the last paragraph of which, I think, is well worth bringing to the attention of hon. members:
Treatment of its Indian wards has long been a scandal in United States politics. Such exploiting as has been shown to exist across the border must never be even hinted at in Canada. Treaties made with the Indians of the Dominion are as sacred as treaties made between nations. The self-respect of Canadians demands that these treaties shall be honoured in better as well as in spirit to their last word.
Before I sit down I would again urge the Superintendent General to cancel this lease. I think it is quite probable that with all the affairs of the Indians and of the other branches of his department bo take care of, he may not have realized at the time the lease was granted just what far-reaching effects it would have and to what extent it was a violation of the treaty entered into by this country with the Indian band. But if he persists in continuing granting the lease in violation of the treaty
Supply-Indian Affairs

I would suggest that the least he could do would be to transfer the lease to that part of the reserve which lies on the north side of the river. Part of the land over there, which was surrendered by the Indians years ago, is unsold and lying, practically idle. I think the consent of the Indians could be easily secured to leasing this part of the reserve. In my opinion it is most unfair to ask the Indians to give up their land which lies close to their camp, the land which they are entitled to use, and compel them to drive their stock over to the north side of the river. As no doubt the Superintendent General knows, the Old Man river at that point is very hard to cross and there are onty a few places where it can be forded. I think it was very unfortunate that the department did not in the first instance deal with that part of the reserve on the north side of the river, if they were determined to grant a lease. Again I appeal to the Superintendent General to do the right and fair thing with these Indians and so convince them of Canada's good faith. Putting the matter on the lowest plane, surely the amount involved is not worth violating the treaty for and arousing distrust and resentment among the Indians. The head chief of the Peigan Indians is a reasonable man and I think all the circumstances of the case go to show that a grave mistake has been made. I do not think that the Superintendent General will be dealing fairly with the Indians or with the country itself if this lease is not cancelled and the prayer of the Indian petition granted.

speechtext: Why the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
A 'ease that is given for sheep is more valuable; you get more money out of it and you can afford to pay more. Moreover, the sheep are more destructive; they graze more closely and destroy the lease very much quicker than the cattle would. The leasing of 150,000 acres of the Blood Indian reserve for that purpose brings in a considerable revenue to the Indians. Not only that, but the Peigan lessee paid $1,800 to the Indians, at the rate of $5 a ton, for the putting up of hay, and besides, the man who looked after the stock assisted also in looking after the Indians' stock. There are 1,700 head of cattle belonging to the Indians in this large area of land. On this reserve, as well as on any other, when the Indians are found to have sufficient stock to oecupy the whole of their territory I would cancel the lease over night. I see no reason why the Indians should not be encouraged to take care of their own cattle, and when they show a disposition to do so I am ready to spend public funds, if no band funds are available, to purchase stock for them. The Indians should make a much greater success as stock men than as agriculturists, although we are trying to teach them agriculture as well. Only 2,877 acres are under cultivation on this whole huge reserve, and there are 385 souls on it, all told. We are not making much of a success in getting the Indians on
Supply-Indian Affairs
that reserve to cultivate their land; but we are making some progress in encouraging them to care for their stock. My hon. friend refers to the winter pasture. It is to be remembered that the location of the Indians is some miles away from the winter pasture; all the way down the valley from the location of the Indians' homes on the north side of the railway is winter pasture. While last winter was a rather mild winter, I venture , to say that the Indians lost fewer cattle during that period than they ever did before; at least that is the report I get from the reserve itself. I am not telling of this in any attempt to justify the breaking of an Indian treaty. I am not making a defence of that sort, but I do want to point out, Just as I pointed out in my letter, that once in a while, if we are going to act in the best interests of the Indians we have to take what may seem like somewhat drastic action. ^
With reference to the ponies my hon. friend referred to, I want to point out that the ponies are roaming east of the Galician reserve, and they are a regular menace to the country. If we ordered them slaughtered there would be an awful row about that, but the best thing that could be done would be to destroy them. They are eating up the grass on the ranches, and are of no value for sale purposes. Anyone in the vicinity knows that it is difficult to sell a work horse, let .alone a pony. These ponies are off the reserve, and as I say, have become a menace.
Let me say with respect to this lease or .any other lease, I am prepared to lend every encouragement, I would even go so far as to recommend loaning to the Indians the *funds of the government for the purpose of .purchasing stock if they would take care of *them.
With reference to statements made by people off the reserves, one of the biggest difficulties we have to contend with is that a few busy gentlemen, largely in the legal profession, make it their business to make a living off these Indians by fomenting grievances. That is a statement I can substantiate by a dozen different cases.

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The minister would not
apply that to Mr. Fawcett who had been mayor of Macleod, and a highly respected gentleman.

speechtext:
I quite
agree with my hon. friend, but all through the country one of the biggest difficulties we have is this fomenting of supposed grievances. The Indian loves to get legal advice. I do not know any white man who is so fond of
Supply-Indian Affairs

taking legal advice as the Indian. He excels his white brother altogether in that line, and very frequently the Indian does not get *good advice. I am not saying that perhaps we have not taken what may seem like drastic action, but I do not think anyone who has lived and dealt with me would say that by disposition or otherwise I would want to coerce or drive anyone into a corner. There are times, however, when in the best interests of these wards of the government, you have to take what may seem at the time drastic action. I think the plains Indians are making splendid progress. I see evidence of it on every hand, and I do think the administration of Mr. Graham has been good administration in that direction. I think we will have a great number of them on the Galician reserve, and on the Blood reserve, where they raised 300,000 bushels of grain last year where very little was raised four or five years ago. The administration of Mr. Faunt, the local agent, has brought about that result. I had to go to the Blood reserve on one occasion accompanied by the deputy superintendent to prevent what looked likely to develop into bloodshed, but after we had spent a day with the chiefs of the band and discussed the matter, we have never had a single bit of disturbance on that reserve since. The trouble arose over supposed injuries; meetings were held, the discontent fomented, and an agitation worked up that eventually forced me to visit the reserve in the interests of the Indians and of the department.
So far as the Peigan reserve is concerned, I have discussed this matter with Chief Big Swan. I pointed out to him that if they had sufficient cattle I would cancel the lease at once, but that the lease was not going to do them any particular damage, and he said it was the principle of the thing he was objecting to, and he was going to keep on objecting to it. That was the statement that he made to me on that occasion. At that time I had Mr. Graham go down there and make a special investigation on his own behalf. He did so, and reported that so far as he could see, the lease from the standpoint of the reserve and the interests of the Indians was a benefit, inasmuch as it brought in SI,300 a year, which, as my hon, friend says, is a small amount, but nevertheless it does help them materially. The cattle on the reserve, some 1,700 head, my hon. friend will readily recognize, have ample grazing territory, in fact, there is grazing for three or four times that number outside altogether of the land that is leased.

I will say this, however, to my hon. friend. So much agitation has been created over this matter that as soon as I reach Alberta, which I hope will be within a few days, seven or eight days at the most, I am going .to Macleod and shall go on the Peigan reserve and meet the chiefs and discuss' this matter with them; and if the grievances are there rvhich they claim exist I shall arrange for the cancelling of the lease. I cannot say anything more in connection with the matter.

speechtext: Would there not be another solution perhaps that would be more worthy of consideration? Sup-ply-Indian Affairs
On the face of it, that looks suspicious. speechtext: Conferences have been held in tie past two or three years with the Indians. My hon. friend will remember that the McKenna-McBride agreement with respect to land has been carried out. We did not entirely satisfy the Indians or their representatives in the allocation of lands, but inasmuch as the provincial government were threatening to cancel the arrangement altogether if we did not take action we thought it well to do something, and the matter between the two governments is settled, although I am bound to say not to the entire satisfaction of the Indians. Regarding the controversy over the aboriginal title, I have been trying for the past three years to find out just what the Indians mean by this. Do they lay claim to all lands in British Columbia in view of the fact that in ninety per cent of the cases no treaty had been signed between the tribes and representatives of the crown? After a great deal of discussion I found that they did not lay claim to the land in its entirety, but they do say that before an adjustment can take place they should have certain specified and unspecified provisions made for them by the government of Canada. This is all so vague and difficult of understanding that it is very hard to arrive at any concrete definition of what their claims are. On behalf of the government I have informed them that we are prepared to do for them everything that was done for treaty Indians in any other part of Canada. As a matter of fact we are giving them the same consideration as we have given every other Indian in Canada. Still that does not seem to be enough; certain claims are made for compensation and so on. I was going to call the

Just at the same time there came a ferry across the river and I saw a man carrying a big mail bag, all he could lug on his back. I went over to see what was in it. It was a large sack of empty mail bags brought across from Rockland on the ferry to Lochaber bay and sent in to Ottawa on the Canadian Pacific. This may be a small thing, but it is these small things that count. I do not see why such expense should be gone to in carrying mail bags into Ottawa. Mail bags are held in cheap estimation and are regarded as being of little account, but just the same they cost money. An effort has been made to save the country a considerable sum of money in the purchase of material for the bags and the manufacture of the bags. This system has been devised. Instead of leaving the bags to be scattered all around the country to be used for the storage of potatoes or the transportation of anything else that needs

transportation and for which another bag is not available, storage depots have been established in different parts of the Dominion with the result-and I am now speaking as to the figures altogether from memory-that last year, the first year this system was in operation, we saved about $157,000 in connection with the purchase of material and manufacture of mail bags. It may be that this package of mail bags which my hon. friend saw, wTas being transferred in the way he says because of the operation of this new system and has no reference to the carriage of the mails or the ordinary operation of the postal service.

No such discrimination exists as regards the railway mail clerks or the letter carriers. They are all treated alike. Further, the work is not of such great difference as to justify this discrimination. The hours of a clerk in grades under seven are just as long and he is, perhaps, expected to be a little bit more acquainted with the work than is the case with the higher grade officers. At any rate,

Here we are asked to vote this sum of money and I cannot see any reason why we should not have all the particulars, especially in view of the fact that the House itself ordered that the information should be brought down. The order of the House was dated June 8. Now we have had this delay from June 8 to the present time. We have an order filed which is incomplete on its face, which shows on its face that the government is not discharging its obligation to the House fairly. I cannot understand, Mr. Chairman, why we cannot get discovery in a case of this kind. We have a right to get it certainly on this vote. speechtext: If this government would only give to other people the opportunity of doing most of their figuring for them, and if they would give to other people the right of directing them and doing something towards having things done in the right way, it would be a grand thing. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I do not see why my
hon. friend should build up such a difficulty. There is no mystery. There is no secret. Mr. Symington has been retained. The amount

of his fees has been given publicly to my hon. friend. It is $200 a, day. It is less than the government of which my hon. friend was a distinquished member paid to the horde of counsel who appeared in the Grand Trunk arbitration and the Canadian National arbitration. It is no secret. This investigation has just taken place. The amount which will be paid will have to be determined by the number of days Mr. Symington has devoted to this work. That has not yet been ascertained. He has not- sent a bill to the department yet. What can we do? I think my hon. friend will agree that we have been busy enough in this House and that we should not be compelled to run after our creditors and ask them to hurry up and send us a bill. He may rest assured that {he bill will be sent in due course, but all that is necessary is to know the amount of the fee, and this has been stated publicly at $200' a day. It will be paid for every day Mr. Symington devoted his time to this inquiry. Why the trouble? Why the fuss? Why is the eloquence of my hon. friend devoted to this subject?

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO AGRICULTURE- LONG TERM LOANS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I do not know whether my hon. friend the Minister of Justice would suggest that orders which the government do not oppose are to be disregarded1. I do not know that he seriously takes that position. It would be much better, however, for my hon. friend to take that position and say that this government is not bound at all by any order of the House, and! that they will pay no attention to it, than to adopt the method they have adpoted here, of bringing down returns which are absolutely illusory and misleading. My hon. friend says there is a lot of fuss being made about nothing. I do not know that it is nothing when a charge is made against an administration that is supposed to function. It is true the supposition is a violent one, but it is certainly not a light charge to say that they treat orders of the House with contempt. We have absolutely no explanation of it one way or the other, but there is a good deal more in this than Mr. Symington's bill. The House said on the 8th June that they were to know, and that a return was to be made as to how much this inquiry would cost, and it would have been a very easy thing to have found out what it would cost. My hon. friend I think knows perfectly well at the present time that the estimate which they have now brought in is not going to cover that cost. Every member of the government knows it perfectly well. It may be that time is unnecessarily wasted about something, but the fault is not here; it is with the government which should have

Retirements jrom Service
paid some attention to the order of the House, instead of putting in a return the only object of which was to mislead the House. I do not consider these idle or light matters. I think the people of this country have a right to regard the formal return of this government as meaning what on its face it is supposed to mean. This return is supposed to cover the whole cost of the inquiry. That is the order, and instead of the order containing that information, it is simply a return which conveniently gives only one item in the whole thing. My hon. friend might say that is right. He may complain about delay, but the delay and the trouble is absolutely owing to the government not doing as they ought to, giving us proper information in connection with an inquiry which I venture to assert will cost-I do not know where it will be hidden- at least $50,000. Why should not at least an estimate be given? I am not asking very much when I ask for an estimate. I simply want an estimate showing how this is arrived at. It seems to be a most outrageous proposition to think that this vote can be put through the House without even a guess as to what it is for, as to whether it is for counsel fees, or for this or that, or whether it is for stenographers, or anything else. I have been letting a lot of things go through this afternoon without saying anything about them, and they were matters which ought to have been discussed. Here is one thing which, if there be any desire to deal honestly with this House and the people of this country, can be answered in two minutes.

I regret to inform the
House that we are losing the services of two 319
distinguished public servants, Mr. Alfred Hamlyn Todd, who after fifty years of service in the library has applied for superannuation on account of ill health, and the other Mr. A. C. Campbell, Editor of Debates. I have received the following letter from Messrs. Burrell and Taehe, Librarians:
Ottawa, June 25, 1925.
The Hon. Rodolphe Lemietjx,
Speaker of the House of Comons.
Sir,-We have the honour to enclose a copy of a report from Dr. Fraser on the condition of Colonel Todd, assistant librarian who has not been able to attend to his duties for some time past. Colonel Todd, we think, recognizes that it will be impossible for him to continue tasks which require the ability to read without difficulty. While reluctant, therefore, to dispense with the services of an official who for more than fifty years has rendered valuable and conscientious services to the library, we respectfully recommend that Colonel Todd be superannuated, and, in view of his unique record, it would be gratifying if he could be given six months' leave of absence with full pay, dating from July 1 next.
We have the honour to be, Sir,
Yours obediently,
M. Burrell.
J. De L. Tache.
I have nothing to add to the compliment paid to Mr. Todd for his long and distinguished services to parliament. I can only express the hope that he may enjoy better health in the future.
As the House has always asserted its authority over its servants, it is moved by Mr. Beland, seconded by Mr. 'Stewart (Argen-teuil):
That this House approves the recommendation of Mr. de L. Tach6, General Librarian, and Honourable Martin Burrell, Parliamentary Librarian, that six months' leave of absence from the first of July, 1925, prior to superannuation, be granted Mr. Alfred Hamlyn Todd, Assistant Librarian, who for more than fifty years has rendered valuable services to the library of parliament.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not
customary to make extended reference to officials of the country on the occasion of their severing their relations with this House, but when a man of the standing and reputation of Cdlonel Todd has passed more than fifty years in the public service and retires, a word of recognition may not be inappropriate. Colonel Todd, as we all know, is the son of a distinguished author who has been of great service himself to parliament. In the performance of his work in the library anyone who frequents that institution will know how uniformly courteous he has always been, how alert and anxious to serve, and how encyclopaedic his knowledge of the library itself. I do not think that in the course of my life

Retirements from Service

as a member I have ever asked for anything in the library which he was not able to reach in very quick time, or for any other service which he was not prompt and efficient to give. I am sure we all regret that he is now encountering ill health and must retire from a work which he liked verj' much indeed. I join with Mr. Speaker in expressing the hope that retirement may prove of benefit to him.
Hon. H. S. BELiAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment): Mr. Speaker, with the greatest of pleasure do I associate myself with the sentiments expressed by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and Your Honour towards Mr. Todd. I remember in my younger days-and it is much longer ago than I care to admit-when I first came to this parliament, almost a quarter of a century ago, I frequently went to the library to read up various subjects and I found Mr. Todd ever ready to guide me in my uncertain steps toward knowledge. I express also, in the name of the government, regret at his being obliged to abandon the position which he has so highly honoured and the duties of which he has discharged with credit to himself, to the House of Commons and to parliament generally. The motion that you have read to the House, Sir, will, I have no doubt, be unanimously approved. It will be only a very feeble recognition of the eminent services rendered by this faithful servant.
Motion agreed to.

As I said a moment ago, another veteran will leave us after this session. I refer to Mr. A. C. Campbell, Editor of Debates, who has been with us in the House of Commons for almost forty years; who was promoted from the press gallery to the floor of the House, and from the floor of the House he ascended further to the office of Editor of Debates. He has always been most attentive to his duties and desirous of helping the members and of facilitating the business of the House of Commons itself. I regret that he has to leave, bu' while expressing that regret the House will learn with pleasure that he will be succeeded by way of promotion by one whom we all know and whom we all appreciate, one who also was a member of the press gallery for many years-I refer to Mr. George Simpson. The total expenses incurred by the special committee in its investigation into Ocean Rates, showing, (a) full amount paid to Mr. Symington in fees, (b) the amount in fees still due to Mr. Symington as counsel, (c) total amount paid and incurred for expenses to Mr. Symington. I want to take advantage of

with the application to develop the power on Spray lakes. Hon. members of the House will have heard of this project before. The situation now is that some two or three years ago the province of Alberta made application in its own right for a license to develop the power in this lake area, which is included in the national parks. An investigation has been carried on, and apparently the consulting engineer employed to advise the government has given the opinion that a great deal of power can be developed in that area. There has been some slight opposition to granting a license in this area on the ground that it would commercialize this section of the park and constitute a very bad precedent. I think hon. members will recall that some of those who have been in that area have indicated very clearly that, so far as scenic value is concerned, the area is not of much significance. A short time ago the government of the province of Alberta called a conference at which representatives of the city of Calgary, the city of Edmonton and some of the other municipalities consulted together with a view of determining whether or not joint action should be undertaken for the purpose of developing this area for water-power purposes. In that connection I desire to read a telegram received) by me under date of June 20, from the mayor of the city of Calgary:
Calgary city council unanimously endorse application Alberta government for rights develop Spray lake power site. Calgary vitally interested not only in question urgent necessity development to meet increased demands for power but proposed storage will effect very considerable floods control Bow river which has often caused serious damage to city in past years. After recent conference with government Edmonton we are satisfied if they are given permit by Dominion authorities there will be no exploitation park resources or disfigurement scenic attractions in national park. City of Calgary by reason its close proximity to Banff park Is deeply concerned in retention of all those things which make park attractive for tourists. We urge your best efforts towards securing of permit by provincial government and hope you will place our views before House on first opportunity.
This is my first opportunity to place before the minister and the House the attitude taken by the city council of Calgary, as indicated by the telegram of its mayor. The only suggestion of opposition to this scheme, so far as I know, is the one reason I have already mentioned, and secondly, a suggestion that perhaps the power can be developed in other parts of the province from coal. I do know but little about the comparative merits of development by steam or water-power; but I do know that the Canmore Coal Company, which is operating a coal mine within a very few miles of the proposed development, has expressed a desire to secure power from this

proposed project for the purpose of carrying on its mining operations. I ask and invite the minister to indicate -to the House his attitude in connection with this important matter, a matter not only of great importance to the city from which I come, but also of great importance to many municipalities of the province, and to the future development of the various sections of the province.

application. I believe a development of this character is somewhat premature but if people want to invest money I do not know that it is any great concern of ours. In the second place, there is no other large development of this character in the province which would yield the same amount of power for the expenditure to be made. I had hoped that the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) would be here to-night. The hon. member takes a vital interest in this question and he is on record in Hansard as registering a mild protest against the exploitation of the parks for any purpose whatever. . I should like to know what the feeling of parliament is on this matter. I intend next session if I am still Minister of the Interior to bring down an amendment to the Paries Act putting the natural resources of the parks under the control of parliament, so that applications of this kind would have to come before parliament in the shape of a bill and be passed upon. There is a very strong feeling abroad that we should not interfere with the natural beauty of the parks and for that reason I think it would be well to place the natural resources of these areas under the control of parliament itself. On the other hand, this application has been pending for three years and I am informed that the provincial government is anxious to go ahead with the development. The Prime Minister so informed me the other day and I assured him that the matter would be discussed shortly in the House when- the estimate was under consideration and when I should have some idea as to how parliament felt about it.

I remember the subject
being before me but very briefly some years ago. I have read the remarks of the minister in a previous debate and, as well, the address of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
I would gather indisputably from his words that he is strongly opposed to anything being done that would mar the natural beauty of this park by any power development at the Spray lakes. I am informed also that there has been considerable protest from other parts of Canada against the general principle of commercializing the parks, and possibly some of these protests have special reference to this site and this projected exploitation. Another factor that weighs with me is the fact, or so I am informed, that the head of the Parks branch, Mr. Harkin, has set his face against the utilization of these falls. On that account it is with some hesitancy that I venture to express an opinion. But finding the government in the position of having no policy it would be a shame not to assist them in any way that one could. I want to

Supply-Interior
say in this respect that their attitude is in no way unique. It is becoming an almost invariable habit with them to represent themselves as being without any opinion on any question that comes up and, as it were, waiting for instructions. Now, I venture the opinion that this country cannot set its face definitely for any length of time against the development of practical power sites in our parks. I do not think that can be done. If you have a big city with aspirations for industrial progress, and hungering for power as Calgary will be, though it may not be just yet, it certainly is assuming a ereat deal to stand a thousand miles away and to say, "Do not harness the power at Spray lakes because I and many others might like to look at the water falling down there. You should be good enough to do without the very life blood of industry in order that we may have that pleasure." I can recall years ago when the question of Niagara development was under review, not in this parliament but in Canada. At that time Canadian and American magazines were filled with protests, with splendidly written articles, and with all sorts of violent protests against the idea of commercializing this wonderful beauty spot of nature. Imagine the folly that would have been .perpetrated had these words been heeded! Just think of the suggestion of denying to the people of Ontario the comforts as well as .the wealth which Niagara development has yielded, in order that some tourists might be able to see more water flowing at a single spot over a hill. Perhaps it is not the same as respects the Spray lakes which are in a natural park. Nevertheless, though perhaps in a lighter degree, the argument applies. There is no province in Canada, unless it be Saskatchewan, which has less natural potential water-power than Alberta; and in that state of the province I do not believe that any government in the world can deny the claims of the people to utilize such powers as they have. Nor is it essential, I should think, that there should be any gross disfigurement of the natural beauty of the park as the result of power development. I know there could be.
They get over that difficulty in Italy and Switzerland and they have great power development.

What the Postmaster
General has been good enough to interject is quite true. By the exercise of careful supervision, power development can be made quite presentable, and if I were in the Banff national park, I would prefer to see there some well executed, splendidly finished engineering feat
that had the purpose of giving to mankind the benefit of a great national asset, to having the mere, crude pleasure of watching the spray at a great height. Consequently, in so far as my advice is of any value to the minister, I would say: Just as soon as he is convinced that there is real use to be made of this power site; that it is really needed, then, subject to proper restrictions, subject to proper supervision, the power should be thrown open. I do not say it should be thrown open to the Calgary Power Company necessarily. It might be the part of wisdom to assign it to the province of Alberta, but I never would assume a dog-in-the-manger policy, and with an affectation for the beautiful in nature, presume to deny to our fellow-beings the use of a great natural possession and resource of Canada.

Certainly one cannot resist
the clear-sighted and logical policy enunciated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). I am sure if he saw some of the snapshots of that area, some of which I have under my hand, he would agree with me immediately that the area has not any very special significance as regards scenic value.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Bow
River says, "hear, hear." He visited that area last year and saw it for himself. That particular variety of scenery can be duplicated in a thousand different places. The parks in Alberta total an area of approximately 9.000 square miles, and all of this, if advocates of park conservation are to have their way, is to be forever a closed area in which there shall be no commercial exploitation at all. Some advocates of park conservation or preservation agree with the view that the parks in Alberta are altogether too large. The present park area should be carefully surveyed so as to pick out the points of special scenic significance, and the rest should foe permitted to be commercialized where commercialization is proper and justified. With what the leader of the opposition says in regard to a proper development especially of this particular area, I find myself in accord. I happen to have a copy of the Manchester Guardian Weekly of Friday, April 17, of this year, and apparently there has been from time to time a great deal of controversy even in England with regard to the preservation of what might be called mountain reservoirs. I desire to read from this article one or two selections which will epitomize the situation:

automobiles do not require a heavy robe of that character, and they are too heavy for coats. We have tried almost everything in the way of manufacturing them with a view to creating a sale for them.
Are they too heavy because of the age of the animal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a very thick hide. It can be stripped and reduced in weight, but still, when manufactured it is much heavier than the ordinary fur coats that are sold nowadays on the market. The old days of the sleigh robe are gone.

What has been the
revenue from the slaughter of the buffalo, and the cost of that slaughter?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The receipts have been about $84,000 as against an expenditure of $76,000. We have in storage hides, heads and pemmican valued at about $161,000.
Item agreed to.

Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil). Certainly.

settlement is fraudulent, and now the item appears in the public accounts as part of the expenditure for administrating the Yukon territory. speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
So far as
I am concerned I do not know anything about this claim. It has certainly never come before the Department of the Interior. My hon. friend states it was in the Exchequer court. I have no recollection of the claim at all. I have a recollection of hearing a claim of this character which had been very long delayed being discussed, but I really am unable to give my hon. friend any information about the matter.

Can the Minister of
Justice do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no recollection
of anything of this kind. It must have been before I took charge of the department. However, I am willing to make a search for it.

It is not very
ancient. The judgment was entered and the money paid after the 1st March, 1924, so it is not much over a year old. I am inclined to think the minister is altogether correct when he says he does not know anything about it, for I could not conceive of him paying this claim if he knew anything about it at all, although the claim does arise entirely out of the administration of the Department of the Interior. What surprises me is that the claim was paid without the minister knowing anything about it. Somebody on behalf of the government must know something about it, and I would like to know the people to whom the money was paid, and why they were paid when they had no claim at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I certainly
will look into the matter. Matters that get into the court for court decision, of course, get out of the hands of the minister except the Minister of Justice. The case is out of the control of the other ministers when it reaches that stage. My hon. friend informs me that the matter has been lying dormant in the Exchequer court for a number of years, and therefore it would not come through the Department of the Interior. However, I shall be very glad to get the information and give it to my hon. friend.

Was the minister made
aware of the settlement of this claim at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My accountant tells me that the payment came through the Department of the Interior, that the judgment was issued, and paid apparently in the ordinary way.
On what date?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In March,
1924.

Does the minister say
that to the best of his recollection the question of consenting to this judgment never came before the government as a whole?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure
it must have come before the government, but I must confess I have no recollection of the matter.

I do not wish in the face of the answer of the minister to make any unfair reference to him, but I do protest against any government consenting to a judgment and then paying the money out on that judgment without coming to parliament. The Exchequer Court Act, of course provides that a judgment of the Exchequer court can be paid merely out of consolidated revenue, but the contemplation of that act was a judgment rendered on the finding of the judge himself, not merely on the approval or finding of the government. It never for a moment was thought it would be a mere means of providing a government with power to pay out public money without recourse to parliament, on the will of the government alone. But that appears to be what was done in this case. If what the hon. member for the Yukon says is right and a judgment was rendered without the mind of the Exchequer court judge being applied to the case at all, if it was done merely on the consent of the government, the government should have come to parliament for authority to pay that money, and there should have been no consent unless parliament approved. It is simply defying the rights of the people.
I do not know anything about the merits of the ease. I am pretty much in the position of the minister. I have a hazy recollection of it, and it is not so hazy after all; it is coming clearer to me, a case amounting to nothing less than a huge magnificent fraud that lay in the Exchequer court for years. I remember it coming before me occasionally, and the very thought of a settlement being spumed, and I am amazed to hear that this government consented to pay out public money to

Supply-Interior
the extent of $100,000 on a claim of that kind. Can anyone tell us who were counsel for the claimants?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot. I was just going to remark that we have a recent case, that of Maunsell, against the Department of the Interior for illegal cancellation of a lease. It comes to my mind because it is recent. I immediately took steps to appeal, to protect our interests in the matter. But the case my hon. friend from the Yukon speaks of, I have no recollection of at all. However, I shall be glad to get the information.

I would like to find out who were the lawyers in this case. While I cannot pretend to any intimacy with the details, the impression that was left on my mind was that the claim was nothing but an unmitigated and colossal scandal.

Would the
minister kindly tell us whether this particular case was handled by the Department of Justice, or whether it was handed out to some political legal friends?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not like to make any statement on the case at all. I have a hazy recollection of the case, at least I think it is the one, but without refreshing my memory with respect to the whole thing, it is difficult to recall any particulars. Undoubtedly the Department of Justice would be handling the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think any agent of the Department of Justice would have agreed to a judgment by consent without the authorization of the department. I do not think this case has come before me while I have been in charge of the department.

I might inform the committee that the solicitors for the suppliant were Aylesworth, Wright, Thompson and Company. The case was never tried by the courts. The government cannot excuse itself by saying it had to carry out a judgment, because the merits of the case were never gone into by the court. It passed through the Exchequer court in the first place on the technical defence which I have outlined to the committee, and was ultimately sent back by the Privy Council to the court for trial on its merits. The merits were never gone into for the reason I suppose that there were no merits. The claim consists of about fifteen items amounting in all to $17,619,000. It reads like a fairy tale, for no one living in Yukon and having seen the ground would say anything but that this claim is absolutely ridiculous. They could not conjure up $2,000,000 let- alone $17,000,000 for the whole lease.

speechtext:

It is done
under our own manager. We have also our own staff.

Is it the old
staff?

speechtext:
We have
Mr. Hays, the former manager, in our employ. He has a large farm in the district and is a thoroughly trained irrigation engineer. speechtext: Yes.
